items.value: Assumptions 1 and 3 are valid: governments and companies must be prepared for climate change, and ignoring it is a huge risk for investors
items.reasoning: Statement 3 is the passage's opening claim in other words — a changing climate and governments' eventual efforts 'could have a big impact on investors' returns', so an investor who ignores climate is carrying an unpriced risk. Statement 1 underlies the rest: governments will act 'however reluctant', and companies face higher taxes, regulatory burdens and stranded assets, so both must be prepared. Statement 2 goes further than the text: the passage says other industries 'could be affected by the economic damage' of extreme weather, which is damage to particular industries, not a claim that weather will reduce the economic growth of governments and companies. Runner-up D (all three): it wins if 'economic damage caused by more extreme weather' is read as equivalent to reduced economic growth. I set it aside because the passage hedges with 'could' and never speaks of governments' growth at all.

items.value: Assumptions 1 and 2 are valid: equality of opportunity is the fundamental goal, and the present school system does not deliver egalitarian education
items.reasoning: Statement 3 is decisive against the other pairings: the passage discusses quotas for weaker sections inside private schools, which presupposes those schools continuing, and it never proposes abolishing them, still less as 'the only way' — so options C and D fall. Statement 2 is supported directly: access to schooling is near-universal but 'access to quality exhibits a sharp gradient with socio-economic status', and equity had been an issue 'that private actors had escaped by and large'. Statement 1 rests on the passage's own phrase, 'the idea of egalitarian education system with equality of opportunity as its primary goal', which is the standard the passage measures private schools against. Runner-up B (2 only): it wins on a strict reading, since that phrase describes the idea of an egalitarian system rather than stating a fact about the Indian education system's fundamental goal.

items.value: Curing TB requires more than diagnosis and medical treatment
items.reasoning: Everything the passage adds beyond the infection itself is non-medical: poverty, insufficient nutrition, unsuitable housing, little understanding of prevention, ostracisation, loss of employment, deep-seated stigma, absent counselling, cost, and lack of support from providers and family — and these together 'demotivate patients to continue treatment — with disastrous health consequences.' That is precisely the claim that medicine alone will not cure TB. A is contradicted, since the passage's concern is treatment being abandoned, not TB being incurable. C invents a surveillance failure and asserts that the poor have no access at all, where the passage says treatment is expensive. D fails on 'only when', an absolute condition the passage never sets.

items.value: Statement 3 alone is sufficient to guarantee that no two consecutive floors share a colour
items.reasoning: Five floors painted in four colours, one colour per floor, means exactly one colour is repeated. Statement 3 puts that repetition on floors I and V: red is used twice there, so floors II, III and IV must carry the three remaining colours, all distinct — which makes every consecutive pair (I-II, II-III, III-IV, IV-V) different automatically. Statement 1 is not sufficient: I and II may share a colour while II, III, IV are still all different, for example red-red-blue-green-yellow. Statement 2 (II different from IV) is weaker still and is already implied by statement 1, so 1 together with 2 adds nothing and option C fails; and since statement 3 works alone, option D's premise that it is insufficient is false. Verified by enumerating all 240 colourings that use all four colours: every one of the 24 satisfying statement 3 meets the goal, while 168 satisfy statement 1 and some fail it.

items.value: 100 km
items.reasoning: Q lies west of P and R lies south of P, so PQ and PR are perpendicular and QR is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 60 and 80. QR = sqrt(60^2 + 80^2) = sqrt(3600 + 6400) = sqrt(10000) = 100 km — the 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 20. Option A (140) is the trap of simply adding the two distances, which would only be right if the towns were collinear.

items.value: Only conclusion 1 is correct — 40 per cent went for both shopping and sightseeing
items.reasoning: The 10 per cent who rested in the hotel did neither activity, so 90 per cent did at least one. By inclusion-exclusion, 80 + 50 - (both) = 90, giving both = 40 per cent, which is conclusion 1. Conclusion 2 then fails: members who shopped only are 80 - 40 = 40 per cent, not 20 per cent. (For completeness, sightseeing only comes to 50 - 40 = 10 per cent, and 40 + 40 + 10 + 10 = 100.)

items.value: None of the three conclusions can be drawn
items.reasoning: The data give only that non-cricketers play football and that every footballer owns a two-wheeler; nothing at all is said about what cricketers own or play. Conclusion 1 fails because the 60 per cent who play cricket are simply unaccounted for — some or all of them may own two-wheelers. Conclusion 2 fails for the same reason in reverse: 'every footballer has a two-wheeler' does not make ownership exclusive to footballers. Conclusion 3 requires the converse of the given conditional — the statement is 'not a cricketer implies a footballer', which leaves a cricketer free to play football as well. Runner-up A (1 and 2 only): it wins if 'a student who does not play cricket plays football' is read as splitting the school into two exclusive groups, which would make conclusion 3 drawable. I set it aside because as printed the sentence is a one-way conditional, and reading its converse into it is the classic error this item appears designed to test.

items.value: 4 such pairs
items.reasoning: Write the number as 10a + b and its reversal as 10b + a. Then 7(10a + b) = 4(10b + a), which reduces to 66a = 33b, that is b = 2a. With a from 1 to 4 (so that b stays a digit) the pairs are 12 and 21, 24 and 42, 36 and 63, 48 and 84 — four pairs, each verified to be in the ratio 4 : 7. A brute-force scan of all two-digit numbers returns exactly these four.

items.value: B scored 380
items.reasoning: The two conditions are B = A - 20 and B = 0.95A. Equating them gives 0.95A = A - 20, so 0.05A = 20 and A = 400, whence B = 380. Check: 380 is 20 less than 400, and 5 per cent of 400 is exactly 20. Option C (400) is A's score, offered as the trap — the question asks for B's.

items.value: 13th January
items.reasoning: A gap of two days between swims means two days pass with no swim, so Seeta swims every third day: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 January. A gap of three days puts Geeta on every fourth day: 1, 5, 9, 13 January. The least common multiple of 3 and 4 is 12, so they coincide 12 days after 1 January, that is 13 January — confirmed by listing both schedules. Runner-up A (7th January): it wins if 'a gap of every 2 days' is read simply as 'every 2 days', giving periods of 2 and 3 days and a meeting on 7 January. I set it aside because the words 'a gap of' should do some work — a gap of two days is two intervening days, as in a school reopening after a gap of two days — and the paper offers both 7th and 13th precisely because the two readings diverge.

items.value: Y gives Z a start of 25 metres
items.reasoning: X giving Y a 40 m start means that when X covers 1000 m, Y has covered 960 m; likewise Z covers 936 m in that same time. Since all speeds are uniform, distances covered in equal time give the speed ratio directly, so Y : Z = 960 : 936. In a 1000 m race between them, when Y finishes, Z has run 1000 x 936/960 = 975 m, so Y can allow Z a start of 1000 - 975 = 25 m. Option A (20) would follow from simply subtracting 40 from 64, which ignores that the starts are measured against X, not against each other.

items.value: (y - x) is less than or equal to 15
items.reasoning: y is at most 40 and x is at least 25, so y - x is at most 40 - 25 = 15, and this bound holds for every admissible pair — option C is always true, with equality exactly at x = 25 and y = 40. Each of the others has a counterexample: A fails at x = 25, y = 40, where x is not greater than y; B fails at x = 100, y = 0, where y - x = -100; D fails at x = 25, y = 0, where x + y = 25. A random search over admissible pairs found counterexamples for A, B and D and none for C.

items.value: 23 years
items.reasoning: Ena is 13, her mother is 24 years older at 37, and her father is three years older than the mother at 40. Ena was born four years after the marriage, so the marriage took place 13 + 4 = 17 years ago, when the father was 40 - 17 = 23. Option C (24) is the trap of using the 24-year gap directly, and option A (22) comes from taking the father as three years younger than the mother rather than older.

items.value: 20 per cent discount
items.reasoning: Rakesh's money is fixed. It bought 8 handsets at the list price and 10 at the discounted price, so 10 x (discounted price) = 8 x (list price), giving discounted price = 0.8 x list price. The reduction is therefore 20 per cent. Option C (25) is the trap of computing the increase in quantity, since 10 is 25 per cent more than 8 — but the discount is measured on price, whose base is different.

An average of 40 over 100 students gives a total of 4000. One score was entered as 83 instead of 53, so the total was overstated by 30; the corrected total is 3970 and the corrected mean is 3970/100 = 39.7. Note the mean must fall, because the wrong entry was too high — which alone rules out D.

items.value: Public research institutions should lead GM technology and set its priorities
items.reasoning: The passage identifies the obstacle as an intellectual property regime creating private monopolies, argues that corporate-driven GM chases short-run profit through herbicide-tolerant and pest-resistant traits whose usefulness is short-lived, and closes by citing the National Farmers Commission that priority should instead go to drought, salinity and other stress tolerance. Since the private agenda is the problem and a different priority is prescribed, the corollary is that public institutions should lead and set the agenda. B (abolishing intellectual property rights through the WTO) and C (barring private corporations from Indian agribusiness) are both far more sweeping than anything the passage argues. D is contrary to the passage, whose first line assumes that 'widespread and careful adoption' of GM is the goal being obstructed.

items.value: Only the assumption that GM companies neglect the effects of natural calamities on agriculture is valid
items.reasoning: Statement 1 follows from the contrast the passage draws: corporations 'make major investments for herbicide-tolerant and pest-resistant crops' because these maximise profit, while the National Farmers Commission has to point out that priority 'must be given' to genes for drought and salinity tolerance — an appeal that only makes sense if such stresses are being neglected. Statement 2 is not assumed: the passage's reason that corporate traits have 'only a short window' is that pests and weeds evolve resistance, which says nothing about GM technology's long-run capacity against global warming, a subject the passage never raises.

items.value: Campaigns against foreign plants are sometimes pointless
items.reasoning: The passage says most invasive species are 'neither terribly successful nor very harmful', that Britain's invasive plants are not widespread, not spreading quickly and are 'often less of a nuisance than vigorous natives such as bracken', and that new arrivals almost always increase diversity while often driving nothing to extinction. Campaigning against a harmless newcomer is therefore sometimes wasted effort — and the hedge 'sometimes' is what keeps C inside the evidence. B overreaches to 'unnecessary' laws, when the passage says most, not all, invaders are benign. A and D turn a description of where invaders settle and what they do into prescriptions to introduce foreign plants deliberately, which the passage nowhere recommends.

items.value: Assumptions 1 and 2 are valid: food safety is complex and needs a multipronged solution, and manpower for surveillance and training needs investment
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is carried by the passage's own list — contaminated groundwater, unsafe agricultural chemicals, poor storage and handling, unhygienic cooking and distribution — described as 'myriad factors that need regulation and monitoring', plus consumer awareness; many causes call for many remedies. Statement 2 follows from surveillance involving several government agencies and entailing 'a good training of inspection staff', together with the closing point that 'investing in training and education of street vendors is of great significance'. Statement 3 fails on both halves: the passage speaks of regulation, monitoring and complaint mechanisms rather than fresh legislation, and its subject is contaminated water, farm chemicals, home and street food — not the food processing industry.

items.value: The passage argues in favour of people's groups participating in city planning
items.reasoning: The complaint is about method: we plan 'via the old ways — the static Development Plan — that draws exclusively from technical expertise, distanced from people's live experiences and needs, and actively excluding large number of people, places, activities and practices'. The named fault is exclusion of people from the process, so the remedy the passage points to is their participation. A blames builders and elites, who are never mentioned. B attacks global and smart cities, also absent from the text. C is close but overstates: the passage says the interests of working and poor people have been neglected, not that cities should be planned mainly for them.

items.value: Only implications 1 and 2 are correct
items.reasoning: Statement 4 is settled at once — the passage says nothing about the rural population's willingness, so options B and D fall; and statement 3 names the service sector, which the passage never mentions, so option C falls, leaving A. The remainder is defensible on its merits: growth accelerating from 3 per cent to 7-8 per cent while organised-sector employment growth halved from 2 per cent to 1 per cent is jobless growth, which implies output is rising through something other than added labour, that is technological progress (statement 1); and with barely 10 percent employed in the organised sector and a vast majority poor, the modern economy is not connecting with labour-intensive, resource-based livelihoods (statement 2).

items.value: Meaningful financial inclusion requires banking correspondents to have diverse skills
items.reasoning: The passage widens what a correspondent must do: banks 'cannot afford to ignore investing in financial education and literacy', and success depends on providers 'who ensure not just basic bank accounts but also products such as accident and life insurance and micro pension schemes'. Teaching financial literacy and selling insurance and pension products alongside deposits is a demand for a range of skills, which is C. A is contradicted, since the passage treats outreach as something that may yet succeed rather than as a failure. B calls for greater numbers, whereas the passage's remedies are costs, training and incentives, not headcount. Runner-up D (multi-bank service): the passage does single out the regulator's one-bank restriction on correspondents 'way too small to be viewed as a systemic risk', so D would win if that were read as the crucial point. I set it aside because D asserts outreach is 'impossible' without it, while the passage makes better incentives generally, not this one change, the condition of success.

The successive differences are -3, -5, -7, -11, -13, whose magnitudes are the consecutive primes 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 — note that 9 is skipped, which is the point of the pattern and rules out reading the gaps as odd numbers. The next prime is 17, so X = 93 - 17 = 76. (Reading the differences as odd numbers would give 93 - 15 = 78, which is not among the options, confirming the prime reading.)

From 8:00 a.m. Monday to 6:00 p.m. Wednesday is 58 hours as shown on the clock's own face, that is 3480 of the clock's minutes. The clock shows 24 h 10 min for every 24 h of true time, so true minutes = shown minutes x 1440/1450, giving 3480 x 144/145 = 3456 minutes = 57 hours 36 minutes. Adding that to 8:00 a.m. Monday gives 8:00 a.m. Wednesday plus 9 h 36 min, that is 5:36 p.m. Wednesday. The correct time must lag the fast clock, so it is before 6:00 p.m., and the lag here is 24 minutes.

items.value: The new fraction is always greater than the original
items.reasoning: Let the proper fraction be a/b with 0 < a < b, and add k > 0 to both parts. Then (a+k)/(b+k) - a/b = [b(a+k) - a(b+k)] / [b(b+k)] = k(b - a) / [b(b+k)], and every factor here is positive because k > 0 and b > a > 0. So the fraction always increases, moving towards 1 — for instance 1/2 becomes 2/3 and 3/4 becomes 4/5. Exhaustive checking of every proper fraction with denominator under 60 and every k up to 39 produced no exception. (The opposite result, A, would hold for an improper fraction, which is why the stem specifies a proper one.)
